title: Our experience in the LA wildfire and TikTok ban
summary: A current-events 'yapping' episode recorded while Jean recovers from pneumonia: the sisters describe living through the January 2025 LA wildfires, the class divide in who gets help, the hidden dangers of urban/structural burn, and the under-the-radar real estate market that followed. They then discuss the looming TikTok ban, Gen Z's migration to RedNote, the Luigi Mangione discourse as a symbol of generational anti-establishment sentiment, and close with movie and TV recommendations.

ideas.idea: Set a concrete, trackable health challenge such as eating 40 different fruits and vegetables a week to make eating intentional.
ideas.detail: Cherie learned the 40-plants-a-week gut-health target from a Delta in-flight masterclass and writes down each qualifying whole food on paper weekly; even without hitting 40, the tracking makes her more mindful and creative in cooking. Herbs, garlic and ginger count.

ideas.idea: Get annual bloodwork done and act on the results with targeted supplements.
ideas.detail: Both sisters got 2025 blood tests showing genetically high cholesterol and borderline vitamin D deficiency; Cherie now takes vitamin D and C, which she says matters even more during wildfire smoke exposure.

ideas.idea: Alarming US health news is usually not doomsday but a delayed catch-up to regulations other countries adopted years earlier.
ideas.detail: Jean argues the FDA red-dye ban and similar stories reflect ingredients already banned in Europe roughly a decade ago; she deliberately buys drugstore skincare and consumables from European, Japanese and Korean brands because those markets have stricter regulation.

ideas.idea: Distinguish health risks you can act on from those you must simply acknowledge and live with, then make your choices.
ideas.detail: Cherie's thorn is doom-scrolling about microplastics in tea bags, red dye, salmonella egg recalls and endocrine disruptors in perfume and dry shampoo; the sisters conclude you act where you can and accept the rest rather than freak out internally.

ideas.idea: Disaster recovery exposes a widening class divide: who gets help depends on the reach of your network, not just the size of your loss.
ideas.detail: West-side Palisades friends raised $40-50K on GoFundMe in three days, while many Altadena families on the east side could not reach $1,000 of a $5,000 goal; Altadena's resources were concentrated on the same block, so the whole community's support system burned at once.

ideas.idea: A fully paid-off family home can be the entirety of a household's net worth, which makes concentrated wealth catastrophic in a disaster.
ideas.detail: For many multigenerational Black families in Altadena the house was their foothold into the middle class and their only generational wealth, with no diversified stock portfolio to fall back on when it burned; Jean cites an NPR segment on this.

ideas.idea: Structural or urban burn is not a normal wildfire, and the AQI you see on your phone does not capture its hazards.
ideas.detail: Many burned houses predate the 1984 asbestos ban, and burned EVs, TVs and laptops release chemicals not measured by AQI; PM2.5 particles were spread by Santa Ana winds of 80-100 mph. An N95 handles brush smoke but nobody knows what is in urban burn.

ideas.idea: Life-saving information in a disaster travels through elite whisper networks, and healthy air should not be a hoarded commodity.
ideas.detail: Jean learned via a screenshot of an Instagram story that Air Doctor was selling $800 hospital-grade purifiers at cost for $150 through a phone line, called six times to get through, and then tried to share it widely because the 99% who need help most are the last to hear.

ideas.idea: After a disaster, the housing market moves off-market: agents go beyond pocket listings to solicit past clients to sell directly to displaced buyers.
ideas.detail: A pocket listing is a home shown to select buyers before hitting the MLS; in post-fire LA, agents were calling old clients who had considered selling in a few years and asking them to sell now to displaced families buying homes or long-term rentals under the radar.

ideas.idea: If you can, house evacuated friends; in a fast-moving fire, situations change within minutes.
ideas.detail: Cherie's gym closed mid-yoga because the Sunset Fire had started seven minutes north, with flames visible behind a Target and CVS; meanwhile the sisters hosted friends evacuated from the Eaton fire who had headaches from the smoke.

ideas.idea: Policy stories like the TikTok ban should be understood through the real people whose livelihoods depend on the platform.
ideas.detail: Cherie, on TikTok since 2020, points to a Forbes article profiling a creator whose entire income is on TikTok; some creators diversify across TikTok, Instagram and YouTube while others are fully dependent. Practical tip: update the app before the ban since delisting stops future updates.

ideas.idea: Gen Z holds two competing tenets, privacy-consciousness and anti-establishment sentiment, and the RedNote migration shows the second winning.
ideas.detail: Jean, who spent 10 years building products for Gen Z, notes users protesting the US government by moving to Xiaohongshu ('Little Red Book', a Mao reference), an app even more directly tied to the Chinese state than ByteDance-owned TikTok, without most knowing or caring about national security.

ideas.idea: The Luigi Mangione discourse marks a tipping point: anti-capitalist, anti-government sentiment now cuts across all socioeconomic classes, unlike Occupy Wall Street.
ideas.detail: Jean was working on Wall Street during Occupy, which felt blue-collar versus white-collar; today's revolt feels like a shared state of mind across classes, echoing 1960s anti-war energy, campus protests and youth protests in South Korea. Five to ten years ago the public would have unanimously called the shooter a monster.

ideas.idea: A symbol becomes powerful when the messenger comes from inside the elite yet still suffered under the system.
ideas.detail: The sisters argue Mangione's wealthy background and UPenn ties made him an 'acceptable' figure for the public to rally behind, while his own back injuries and medical bills showed even the moderately wealthy cannot escape the healthcare system; they were still disturbed by the lionizing rhetoric.

ideas.idea: The 'Gen Z doesn't want to work' stereotype does not match the Zillennials the sisters know in tech, who are establishment-minded.
ideas.detail: Cherie says her Ivy League friends in consulting, finance and PE skew millennial, are drawn to capitalism and work extremely hard, so the generalization has not shown up in her circle.

ideas.idea: Excessive media exposure of an actor's real personality undermines their ability to disappear into a role.
ideas.detail: Reviewing A Complete Unknown (they rate it about 6.5 versus 7.8 on IMDb), Jean felt Timothee Chalamet's giggles broke character, comparing him to Brad Pitt and George Clooney, whereas Cillian Murphy's avoidance of press preserves mystery that helps audiences suspend disbelief.

ideas.idea: First-generation Americans can lack the shared cultural references that multigenerational families absorb at home.
ideas.detail: Cherie recognized zero Bob Dylan songs in the film because her immigrant parents never played that music at home; she grew up on Britney Spears and NSYNC, which shaped why the biopic did not land for her.

ideas.idea: Escapist, well-crafted TV is a legitimate tool to turn your brain off during emotionally heavy news cycles.
ideas.detail: They recommend Yellowstone ('cowboy Succession' with nuanced Native American storylines and beautiful cinematography), Love Island All Stars and The Traitors as low-effort relief, and Severance and Black Mirror (episodes Hang the DJ, USS Callister, White Christmas) for thought-provoking viewing.
